Permutation test for a Solomon contrast

Source: R/solomon_core.R
perm_solomon.Rd

Performs a randomization-based test by permuting treatment assignment within pretest strata. This preserves the Solomon four-group design while generating the null distribution for a selected treatment contrast. Participants are permuted in unclustered designs and whole clusters in clustered ones.

Usage

perm_solomon(
  fit,
  contrast = "ATE (avg over pretest)",
  reps = 5000L,
  seed = NULL,
  return_dist = FALSE,
  statistic = c("studentized", "difference"),
  object = deprecated()
)

Arguments

fit

An object returned by fit_solomon_glm(). Designs with several treatments are not supported; see fit_solomon_glm().

contrast

Character string identifying the contrast to test. One of "ATE (avg over pretest)", "Pretest x Treatment", "Treatment | pretested", or "Treatment | unpretested". The pretest effects of the fit are not tested: permuting treatment labels says nothing about them, and with a pretest covariate the pretest labels cannot be permuted. For a binary fit with a pretest covariate on a noncollapsible link such as the logit, "Pretest x Treatment" gives a classed warning (solomonR_link_scale_warning): on that scale the contrast is nonzero whenever the pretest predicts the outcome, even without sensitization (Daniel et al., 2021), so a rejection need not reflect sensitization; see marginal_solomon().

reps

Number of permutations. Default is 5000. In clustered designs with at most reps possible allocations, every allocation is used.

seed

Optional random-number seed for reproducibility. The global random-number state is restored when the function exits. In clustered designs, the clusters are taken in the C locale's order of their IDs (the order of the characters' Unicode code points, in which capital letters come before lower-case ones and accented letters after both), whatever the session's collation; a factor cluster is taken by its labels in that order, not by its level order. The IDs are not changed: text as read.csv() returns it is taken by its bytes, which gives that order for a UTF-8 file in any session. So a seed gives the same allocations in every session.

return_dist

Logical. If TRUE, return the permutation distribution in addition to the observed statistic and p-value.

statistic

"studentized" (the default, and recommended) divides the contrast by its standard error; "difference" uses the contrast itself, which tests only the sharp null hypothesis (see "The difference statistic").

object

Use fit.

Value

An object of class solomon_perm, a list with:

  • contrast: the label of the contrast tested.

  • statistic: the statistic permuted, "studentized" or "difference".

  • level: the level permuted, "participant" or "cluster".

  • estimate: the estimated contrast.

  • z_obs: the observed statistic (the contrast itself when statistic = "difference"); Inf when the observed labels give an infinite statistic (see "Degenerate permutations").

  • p_perm: the permutation p-value.

  • reps and valid_reps: the number of permutations, and the number used, which counts infinite statistics and not the permutations left out.

  • exact: whether every possible allocation was used.

  • n_infinite and n_left_out: the number of permutations used whose statistic is infinite, and the number left out.

  • n_classes: the number of classes of permutations whose statistic was computed, for unclustered fits.

  • tie_tolerance and tie_scale: the tie window and the unit's floor with which ties were counted (see "Ties"); plot_perm() uses them.

  • design, n_allocations (the number of possible allocations), min_p (the smallest attainable p-value when exact), and clusters (the numbers of treated and control clusters in each stratum), for clustered fits.

  • z_perm: with return_dist = TRUE, the permuted statistics, one per permutation in the order drawn (one per allocation when every allocation was used): NA for a permutation left out, Inf for an infinite statistic.

The result tests one contrast and gives no interval, so it has no effects table; see solomon_output.

Details

Supported models. perm_solomon() supports the four models the package documents and validates: the Gaussian (identity link), binomial (logit link), and Poisson (log link) models, and family = "negative_binomial" (MASS::glm.nb(); Venables & Ripley, 2002). Any other family or link stops with an error of class solomonR_perm_family_error, at the participant and the cluster level; the review of issue #132 found p-values too small with other links (issue #134). A quasi-binomial or quasi-Poisson model gives the coefficients and HC3 standard errors of its parent family, so refit it with binomial() or poisson(); refit a MASS::negative.binomial(theta) model with family = "negative_binomial". Every error of perm_solomon() named below also has the class solomonR_perm_error.

Unclustered designs. Treatment labels of participants are permuted within pretest strata, among the participants in the model, and the model is refitted for each permutation. A participant outside the model (a missing posttest, covariate, or treatment) enters no refit and is not permuted, so each pretest condition of the model keeps its numbers of treated and control participants, as randomized. The default statistic is the HC3-studentized contrast (MacKinnon & White, 1985). The permutation p-value is a valid test of the sharp null hypothesis that treatment has no effect for any participant; the +1 correction keeps the Monte Carlo p-value from being zero (Phipson & Smyth, 2010). That result is for the count of permuted statistics at least as extreme as the observed one, so a permutation whose statistic equals the observed one is counted. Studentizing the statistic makes permutation tests asymptotically robust when only an average effect is hypothesized to be zero (DiCiccio & Romano, 2017; Wu & Ding, 2021); for the Pretest x Treatment contrast that robustness should be regarded as approximate.

Ties. A permutation ties with the observed one when it repeats the observed assignment or swaps arms of equal size, and often when scores are tied, as with binary outcomes, counts, and ratings. Ties are found by structure first. Permutations that give each arm the same participants as the model sees them (the same outcome, covariates, and exposure) form one class, whose statistic is computed once; a permutation that swaps the arms of a pretest condition gets the statistic of its swap with the sign reversed, and a class that is its own swap gets exactly 0. Each refit is taken to the exact maximum-likelihood estimate by Newton's method, with the HC3 variance computed from the weights at that estimate, as the sandwich package computes it for a generalized linear model (Zeileis, 2006). The outcome of a Gaussian fit and any matrix covariate are moved by one of their own values before the refits, a subtraction that is exact for values within a factor of two of it (Higham, 2002, Theorem 2.5); numeric covariates and the pretest are standardized as for the fit's inference. So scores and covariates far from zero give the same p-value.

Statistics that structure does not tie, but that are equal in exact arithmetic, are counted as ties within a window measured on each call: 100 times the largest rounding error of the observed statistic and of the distinct permuted statistics within a relative 1e-6 of it, each measured as the change when its model is refitted with the rows in reverse order. The window is relative to the larger of the observed statistic and a unit, and is never below 2^-40. The unit is 1 for the studentized statistic; for the difference statistic it is the largest permuted difference, but at least the outcome's standard deviation for a Gaussian fit and 1 for the logit and log links. The result records the window as tie_tolerance and the unit's floor as tie_scale. A classed warning (solomonR_perm_margin_warning) says when the count rests on a numerical margin: a distinct permuted statistic below the window but within 100 windows of it, a window wider than a relative 1e-7, or a permutation classified close to one of the thresholds given under "Limits".

Degenerate permutations. Each permutation, the observed labels included, is classified in this order:

  • With the studentized statistic, a participant at leverage 1 whose HC3 term enters the contrast's variance (an arm of one participant, or a covariate value that no one else in the cell shares) leaves the HC3 standard error undefined, so the test stops with solomonR_perm_leverage_error, which names the permutation; use statistic = "difference". An arm of one has one participant under every permutation, so the test then stops at the observed labels.

  • A permutation under which a covariate collinear with the cells leaves the contrast not estimable is left out, even when it empties an arm, and so is one whose model cannot be refitted; n_left_out counts both. A collinear permutation under which the contrast stays estimable is kept, with the aliased coefficient set to 0. When the observed contrast is not estimable, or every permutation is left out, the test stops with solomonR_perm_estimable_error.

  • An emptied arm (no events, or only events, in a cell the contrast uses, so that the estimate does not exist; Albert & Anderson, 1984), separation by a covariate, and constant arms (an HC3 variance of 0 with a contrast that is not 0) give an infinite statistic, counted as at least as extreme as any other, for both statistics. So do two emptied arms whose infinite parts have opposite signs. An infinite observed statistic gives the share of permutations whose statistic is also infinite.

  • A contrast of exactly 0 with no spread counts as 0.

  • A degenerate cell that the contrast does not use takes the value of the limiting model (Geyer, 2009).

A classed warning (solomonR_perm_infinite_warning) says when half or more of the permutations used have an infinite statistic, since p cannot then fall below (k + 1) / (m + 1), and another (solomonR_perm_convergence_warning) when a refit failed or did not converge.

No variation. When the outcome, and any exposure, takes one value among the participants in the model in a pretest condition that the contrast uses, the test stops with solomonR_perm_no_variation_error if the contrast is 0 or undefined under every permutation: when the contrast is on that condition alone, or the outcome is at its bound (no events, or only events). Otherwise the contrast still varies, through the other condition, a covariate the conditions share, or the exposure, and the test gives its p-value with a classed warning (solomonR_perm_no_variation_warning) that names the condition.

The difference statistic. statistic = "difference" tests only the sharp null hypothesis. A permutation test of a difference in means is exact when the two arms' outcomes have the same distribution, but when only the average effect is zero it keeps its level, even asymptotically, only if the arms are equal in size or in variance (Romano, 1990). In a check for issue #113 (1,000 replications of 199 permutations; the average treatment effect; 8 treated and 24 control participants in each pretest condition; a treated standard deviation twice the control one; no effect), the Type I error at .05 was 0.144 (Monte Carlo standard error 0.011) for the difference statistic and 0.064 (0.008) for the studentized statistic. A classed warning (solomonR_unbalanced_arms_warning) is therefore given when the difference statistic is chosen and treated and control participants differ in number in a pretest condition that the contrast uses. The studentized default is recommended.

Clustered designs. Randomization inference must permute the unit that was randomized, so for fits with a cluster variable the treatment labels of whole clusters are permuted. Two assignment mechanisms are supported:

  • whole clusters assigned to the four Solomon conditions, as in Kvalem et al. (1996), where treatment labels are permuted among clusters within each pretest condition; and

  • treatment assigned to clusters and pretesting to participants within clusters, where treatment labels are permuted among all clusters and every cluster must contain pretested and unpretested participants.

Designs that assign treatment to participants within clusters are refused, and stratified or restricted randomization of clusters is not supported. A cluster ID that is missing (NA), empty (""), or only white space for a participant in the model is refused with an error of class solomonR_cluster_error. The CR2 fits of fit_solomon_glm() refuse such an ID too, but a fit with a cluster and another covariance can hold one, as can a fit made by an earlier version of solomonR.

The statistic is built from cluster-level summaries (Gail et al., 1996; Hayes & Moulton, 2017, ch. 10). A Stage 1 model with every term of the fit except treatment (the pretest indicator, the pretest score, covariates and any exposure offset) gives each cluster a covariate-adjusted difference residual: observed minus expected, divided by the number of participants or, for counts, by the total exposure (Hayes & Moulton, 2017, pp. 221–224, following Bennett et al., 2002). Because Stage 1 ignores treatment, the test remains exact under the sharp null hypothesis. When pretesting is assigned within clusters, each cluster has a pretested and an unpretested residual, and each contrast compares treated and control clusters on one combination of the two.

The contrast is estimated from unweighted means of the cluster residuals, so each cluster counts once (Hayes & Moulton, 2017, pp. 202–205). It therefore estimates the average effect across clusters, which can differ from the participant-weighted contrast of fit_solomon_glm() when cluster sizes vary and effects depend on cluster size. The studentized statistic divides the contrast by its separate-variances standard error (Hayes & Moulton, 2017, p. 212), which is the studentization Wu and Ding (2021) use for weak null hypotheses, applied here with clusters as the units. Gail et al. (1996, p. 1079) showed that the unstudentized difference can exceed the nominal level under the weak null hypothesis when the arms have unequal numbers of clusters and unequal variances.

Stage 1 is fitted to the covariates and pretest standardized as for the fit's inference, so covariates far from zero give the same p-value. Statistics that differ by less than a relative 1e-10 are counted as ties, relative to the larger of the observed statistic and, for the difference statistic, the largest permuted difference (1 for the studentized one); the result records tie_tolerance = 1e-10 and tie_scale = 0. Arms whose variance is at most 1e-10 times the variance the contrast would have if each arm's scores varied as their stratum's do are constant: the studentized statistic is then infinite, counted as at least as extreme, or 0 when the contrast is within 1e-8 of 0 on that scale, and an infinite observed statistic gives the share of allocations whose statistic is also infinite. When the cluster scores do not vary in any stratum the contrast uses, the test stops with solomonR_perm_no_variation_error; when they do not vary in one of two, it gives the p-value with solomonR_perm_no_variation_warning. A negative binomial fit with HC3 standard errors is permuted at the cluster level too, with Stage 1 at the fit's theta; the simulation below does not cover it.

When the number of possible allocations is at most reps, all of them are enumerated and the p-value is exact; the smallest attainable p-value is then reported. Hayes and Moulton (2017, p. 239) note that at least four clusters per arm are needed for a two-sided p below .05.

Simulation evidence. In the package's pre-registered simulation study (issue #19; 96 scenarios, 2,000 replications each):

  • Under the sharp null hypothesis, both statistics had Type I errors of at most 0.063, consistent with the exactness of randomization tests. With four clusters per arm, few allocations exist and the test is conservative: the attainable level at .05 is 2/70, about 0.03.

  • When treatment made treated clusters four times as variable as control clusters, so that only the average effect was zero, the studentized statistic's Type I error reached 0.065 with equal numbers of treated and control clusters, 0.0685 with 15 treated and 47 control clusters per pretest condition, and 0.0805 with 4 and 8. The difference statistic reached 0.158 with 15 and 47, as Gail et al. (1996) found for unbalanced designs. A classed warning (solomonR_unbalanced_clusters_warning) is therefore given, for either statistic, whenever treated and control clusters differ in number. It also has the class solomonR_unbalanced_arms_warning of the participant-level warning, so one handler can catch both.

  • The CR2 tests of fit_solomon_glm() reached 0.068 with four clusters per arm even under the sharp null, where this test is exact, so the permutation test is preferred for designs with few clusters.

Limits. The counts are checked exactly against a reference set of p-values fixed before these rules were chosen (issue #134). What remains:

  • The classification rests on thresholds, not certificates: leverage 1 at a hat value above 1 - 1e-8; a contrast not estimable when its component in the null space of the design exceeds 1e-7 (the tolerance of the pivoted QR decomposition); a zero HC3 variance at 1e-20 of the model-based variance of the contrast (times the outcome's variance for a Gaussian fit), and a zero contrast at 1e-10 of its square root; and separation when the linear predictor of a row still moves by more than 1e-3 per Newton step toward its bound. Only emptied arms are decided exactly, from counts. The margin warning marks a decision near its threshold, on the side the decision went to: a null-space component in (1e-7, 1e-4], a leverage in (1 - 1e-5, 1 - 1e-8], a contrast in (1e-10, 1e-7] of its scale when the variance is 0, a variance in (1e-20, 1e-14] of its scale, a Newton step in (1e-6, 1e-3], and a row set aside while moving by less than 0.1 per step. It makes such a decision visible; it does not make it right.

  • The tie window is a margin rule: the rounding error it rests on is an estimate, not a bound. An ill-conditioned design widens it, and the margin warning then says so. Two classes that are equal only in mirrored data (factor levels exchanged and a binary outcome recoded) are tied only within the window.

  • With the studentized statistic, leverage 1 that a covariate creates can arise under some permutations and not others, so whether the test stops can depend on the seed.

  • The negative binomial's theta is fixed at the fit's estimate in every refit. When the fit warned that theta did not converge (solomonR_theta_boundary_warning), the test proceeds at that estimate; no reference p-value covers that case, at either level.

  • The reference set has gaps, listed on issue #134. It does not include missing treatment values; three of the issue's own data sets (the package's tests check two of them); a Poisson first stage far from zero in the clustered test; a search for mirrored data; observed statistics chosen to be exactly 0 or in the most extreme class (such statistics occur in it, but were not targeted); or a negative binomial near-tie whose gap exceeds the rounding error of solomonR 0.8.2's statistic. Three of its own steps rest on tolerances rather than proofs: ordering the classes whose statistics it computed in doubles, placing exact zeros below the observed statistic, and taking a Poisson or negative binomial fit as exact only when its residuals are below 1e-6.

  • solomonR 0.8.2 and earlier permuted the labels of participants outside the model, so for data with missing values the p-values, and the permutations a seed draws, differ from those releases.

Examples

fit <- with(solomon_example, fit_solomon_glm(y_post, treat, pretested, y_pre))
# Few permutations keep the example fast; use the default for analyses.
perm_solomon(fit, reps = 199, seed = 1)
#> Solomon randomization test
#> --------------------------
#> Contrast: ATE (avg over pretest)
#> Estimate: 2.66
#> Observed studentized statistic: z = 1.68
#> Permutation p = .090
#> Permutations used: 199 of 199
